title: Scrape burnt pancakes off a griddle over the lip into its grease tray with a scraper
instruction: Scrape the griddle clean into the grease tray with the scraper.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00, about 670,000 US jobs, BLS) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00, about 1.4 million) scrape the griddle between orders and at close. O*NET's tasks for fast food cooks include "Clean food preparation areas, cooking surfaces, and utensils" and "Operate large-volume cooking equipment, such as grills, deep-fat fryers, or griddles"; for restaurant cooks, "Inspect and clean food preparation areas, such as equipment, work surfaces, and serving areas". At breakfast, pancakes left on the heat while an order goes out burn onto the plate, and burnt food left there burns onto the next order. It is stuck to the steel, so the scraper's edge has to be held flat on the plate and driven into it to break it up; a lifted edge rides over it. What it pushes spills round the blade's ends, so strokes have to overlap, and the pile has to be pushed over the lip into the tray, not flicked off onto the line.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Griddle: an Assure Parts 177AOGT1227 range-top add-on griddle (27 x 12-1/4 in. overall; a 22-3/8 x 12-1/4 in. (56.8 x 31.1 cm) cooking surface of 7-gauge type 430 stainless; 1-1/2 in. (3.8 cm) splash guards on both sides and the far end; a 3 x 12-1/4 x 1-1/4 in. grease tray across the open near end), set on the bench on its frame with the plate's top 5.0 cm above the bench and clamped down (fixed), tray end toward the robot. The plate runs from x 15.0 (the lip over the tray) to 71.8 and from y -17.55 to 13.55. The tray runs from x 7.4 to 15.0, its floor 3.2 cm below the plate's top. The plate is seasoned and lightly greased, as a working griddle is (in real trials 1.00 g of oil wiped on and buffed off to a film of at most 0.10 g). The frame sits against two stop blocks on the bench (the plate's near right corner within 2 mm, the lip square within 0.5 degree, the plate's top 5.0 cm up within 2 mm and level). (2) Debris: four burnt silver-dollar pancakes stuck to the plate, 7.0 cm across and 5 mm thick, 30.8 g in all (0.5 g per cubic cm, porous char). They were cooked in four of the seven 2.75 in. (7 cm) cavities of a Norpro 957R silicone silver-dollar pancake mold: two side by side, their near edges 1.0 cm from the lip (centers x 19.5, y -7.5 and 0.5), and two behind them, offset half a cavity (x 26.4, y -3.5 and 4.5). Each pancake is cracked into 22 fragments (about 1.2 cm across, 1 mm cracks), each bonded to the plate on its own and freed when pushed sideways harder than 12 N per m of its width across the stroke (0.11 to 0.21 N); once free it slides on the greased plate. The layout is the same every trial. In real trials the debris is cooked the same way every trial (README): with the plate cold, the mold is set square with its two near cavities' edges 1.0 cm from the lip and the right one's edge 6.55 cm from the right guard (6 in. steel rule, within 2 mm); on a range away from the robot the plate is heated to 190 degrees C (375 F, the mix box's griddle temperature, six points on a surface thermometer); batter of Krusteaz Light & Fluffy Buttermilk Complete Pancake Mix, mixed per the box (1 cup of mix to two-thirds of a cup (158 g) of cold water, rested 2 minutes), is weighed into the four cavities and a fifth (the witness), 15.0 g each; after 2 minutes the mold is lifted off, the plate is held at 232 degrees C (450 F) for 20 minutes so the pancakes burn on, and cooled to under 40 degrees C. A batch is used only when the witness pancake's mass and every pancake's black area on the top photo match the reference set in the first three batches. (3) Scraper: a Dexter-Russell Basics P94850 4 in. griddle scraper: stiff stainless blade 10.2 cm wide (1.5 mm thick in the simulator), 21.6 cm overall, white polypropylene handle 11.4 cm long (3.0 x 2.4 cm in the simulator) in line with the blade, 136 g. It lies loose on the bench right of the griddle, edge toward the robot, resting on its edge and the handle's end, centered at x 25.0, y -25.5 (in real trials laid in an outline traced on the bench, within 5 mm and 3 degrees). Both arms start at their ready pose. The griddle is cold and off the range: the trial runs cold so the robot and operator work next to a plate at room temperature and every trial starts at the same temperature (cooks scrape it warm).
scoring: Measured by mass, as shares of the debris (30.8 g in the simulator), from where each fragment ends up. In the tray means inside the tray's walls and below the plate's top. Off the griddle means outside its footprint (plate, tray and splash guards): on the bench, the floor, or carried off on the scraper. Everything else is left on the griddle. The trial scores 1.0 when at least 98% is in the tray and at most 2% is left on the griddle (the plate is clean: 2% is about one fragment, each 0.8 to 1.7%), and the scraper has been set down on the bench off the griddle, released and still for 1 s. Set down: the point where its neck meets the handle less than 3 cm above the bench and outside the griddle's footprint; released: no gripper touching it; still: under 1 cm a second and 10 degrees a second. The job is not finished while the scraper is still in hand or lying on the griddle. It scores 0.75 when at least 90% is in the tray and at most 5% is left on the griddle (about a fifth of a pancake). It scores 0.5 when at least 60% is in the tray, and 0.25 when at least 25% is (about one pancake). Otherwise it scores 0. Doing nothing scores 0. Two caps apply to every score. More than 2% off the griddle (a fragment or two thrown onto the line) caps the score at 0.25. A gouge caps it at 0.5 for the rest of the trial: while the scraper is held and sliding with its edge on the plate (within 0.6 mm, about the simulator's resting gap; 1.0 mm once a stroke has begun), the blade over 70 degrees to the plate, or its edge tilted over 10 degrees so only one corner touches, for 1 cm or more of a stroke (a stand-in for chatter marks in the seasoning). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial the same shares are weighed on an Ohaus Scout STX2202 balance (0.01 g): the tray's gain (in the tray); what is lifted off the plate, guards and blade with a razor scraper and brush (left on the griddle); what is brushed off the catch sheets, bench, floor and scraper (off the griddle). Their sum is the total; a trial whose total is more than 10% off four times the batch's witness pancake is repeated. The set-down is judged from the video. Top photos before and after, from a fixed overhead phone under a fixed raking light with a 1 cm grid, record what is left; a new scratch 1 cm or longer is the gouge.
reset_notes: Empty, wash, dry and weigh the tray. Scrape, wipe and dry the plate until its grid photo shows no particle 1 mm or larger (re-season every 10 trials). Re-grease (1.00 g of oil buffed to at most 0.10 g), set the mold at its marks, cook and burn a fresh batch, cool it to under 40 degrees C, and accept it on its batch check (README). Clamp the griddle against its stops and lay the scraper in its outline. In simulation every trial starts with every fragment bonded in place and the tray empty.
fidelity: Real size. Each pancake is 22 rigid fragments, each held by a breakable joint freed when the blade pushes past 12 N per m of its width (baked food soils on steel: 0.3 to 80 J/m2), standing in for the real burnt pancakes, checked by mass and black area each batch. Sim pancake 7.7 g, real about 7 g (estimated); both scored by share. Friction: greased plate 0.15 to 0.2, char on steel 0.4 to 0.5. No heat. Rigid scraper. Gouge: a blade-angle rule.
